title: Height of vertebral spines is proportional to the local bending moment

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Height of vertebral spines is proportional to the local bending moment

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In the vertebral girder, ligaments form the upper tension member, vertebral bodies the lower compression member and the spines the web, and the height of the vertebral spines at each point along the back is proportional to the bending moment at that point.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: height of vertebral spine h(x) \propto bending moment M(x)

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: secondly we observe that the depth of the web, or distance apart of the principal members,—that is to say the height of the vertebral spines,—must be proportional to the bending-moment at each point along the length of the girder.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XVI, “On Form and Mechanical Efficiency”; topic “Vertebral spines and bending moments”. Scope: vertebral columns of quadrupedal and bipedal vertebrates

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: height of vertebral spine h(x) \propto bending moment M(x)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch16-10: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.67

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The proportionality is explicit and morphology is well represented in public scans. Functional loading is not paired with most specimens and plausible leverage alternatives reduce discrimination.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure neural-spine height along reconstructed vertebral columns, calculate local bending moments for standardized postures, and test proportionality within and across species. Alternative models based on muscle leverage should be compared.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Spines also serve muscle attachment and stabilization.

Moment profiles require uncertain body-mass and muscle-force estimates.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.7
data adequacy: 0.45
analysis feasibility: 0.65
data existence: 0.65
operationalizability: 0.9

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Spine height is directly measurable on open CT once a bending-moment model is specified. That model is the cantilever picture of the preceding claim, so errors in mass distribution carry into the regression. A comparative sample can test proportionality in well-studied species and will confound mechanical moment with muscle attachment area.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure neural-spine height at each vertebra and regress it on the bending moment predicted from body-segment masses and the positions of the limb supports. A positive proportional fit would support the claim; spine height that follows muscle size or display with no relation to the moment diagram would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Tall spines also anchor ligaments and epaxial muscles and, in some species, display structures.

Segment masses and support points are only partly available in the same files as the skeletons.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

data existence: 0.58
discriminating power: 0.55
data adequacy: 0.45
analysis feasibility: 0.5
